Macroeconomic.title: Iran sought permission for docking of 3 ships in Indian ports; approval granted: EAM Jaishankar
Macroeconomic.content:
Iran sought India’s permission on February 28 for three ships to dock at Indian ports, and approval was granted on March 1. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar disclosed in Parliament that IRIS LAVAN docked in Kochi on March 4, with its crew housed in Indian naval facilities. This marked the first time a senior Indian official confirmed Iran requested docking for three vessels. One of the three warships, IRIS Dena, was torpedoed and sunk by a US submarine on March 4 while returning from the Milan multilateral naval exercise and India’s International Fleet Review; at least 87 Iranian sailors were killed. Another Iranian vessel, IRIS Bushehr, sought entry into Sri Lankan waters and was approved to dock at Sri Lanka’s eastern port of Trincomalee.

Jaishankar tied these developments to India’s energy security, noting that global energy supplies have faced disruptions amid escalating West Asia tensions. He stressed the government’s commitment to energy security, prioritizing Indian consumers, balancing availability, costs, and risks, and supporting energy enterprises through diplomacy when needed. He also described advisories issued by Indian embassies in Israel, Iran, the UAE, Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia between February 28 and March 8.

Jaishankar highlighted the regional stakes for India, including the presence of about one crore Indian citizens in the Gulf and a few thousand Indians in Iran, underscoring the West Asian conflict’s implications for oil and gas supplies. The declarations came as Sri Lanka allowed IRIS Bushehr to dock in Trincomalee, illustrating broader regional naval activity amid tensions.

Macroeconomic.title: Two Indian ships cross Strait of Hormuz as Iran says it allowed passage
Macroeconomic.content:
Two Indian-flagged LPG tankers crossed the Strait of Hormuz early Saturday morning and are en route to India, the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways said, marking a rare passage as Iran has largely halted Hormuz traffic after the late-February start of a conflict involving the US and Israel. Tehran has signaled it will not allow supplies for the US or its allies to leave the strait, but India sought and appeared to obtain exemptions. Iran’s ambassador to India, Mohammad Fathali, told a New Delhi India Today conclave that some Indian vessels were allowed safe passage, though he did not specify the number of ships.

The development comes amid a critical cooking-gas shortage in India tied to the regional conflict. About 20% of global oil and seaborne LNG passes through Hormuz. Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday about transit of goods and energy from the Gulf.

In response to the shortage, India’s government invoked emergency powers, directing refiners to maximize LPG production and cutting sales to industry to protect supplies for 333 million homes with LPG connections. It also urged LPG users to avoid panic buying and consider switching to piped natural gas (PNG) where possible. The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas announced on Saturday that it has barred PNG-connected consumers from retaining, obtaining or refilling domestic LPG cylinders under an amended supply order, and prohibited government oil companies from providing LPG connections or refills to PNG-connected consumers.

Macroeconomic.title: EU, India focus on implementing FTA, defence deal: Ursula von der Leyen
Macroeconomic.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU and India are now focused on efficiently implementing their recently concluded Free Trade Agreement (FTA) and Security and Defence Partnership, signed after the January 27 summit between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and EU leadership. The comments came after a meeting with Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, who is in Brussels on a two-day visit. Jaishankar’s trip marks the first high-level Indian visit to Brussels since the landmark deal was finalised; he traveled to the Belgian capital on Sunday at the invitation of EU High Representative and Vice President Kaja Kallas. Von der Leyen called the FTA the “mother of all deals” and said rapid implementation is needed to deliver benefits for people in Europe and India as soon as possible. The discussions also touched on West Asia and Ukraine, with de-escalation, stability and energy security cited as shared objectives.

The EU, as a bloc, is India’s largest trading partner in goods. For FY 2024-25, India’s total trade in goods with the EU was about USD 136 billion, with exports of USD 76 billion and imports of USD 60 billion. The partnership was framed as not only a major trade deal but also a robust security and defence collaboration.

Civil.title: GE Aerospace to Invest Another $1B in U.S. Manufacturing
Civil.content:
GE Aerospace announced on March 9, 2026 that it will invest another $1 billion in U.S. manufacturing in 2026, its second consecutive $1B U.S. investment. The funding will span sites in more than 30 communities across 17 states and support the supplier base, with plans to hire 5,000 U.S. workers in addition to the 5,000 hired last year.

Key allocations include:
- Accelerating engine deliveries and maintenance readiness: $115 million in Cincinnati, Ohio (GE’s HQ) to modernize infrastructure, increase test cell capacity, and expand advanced 3D metal printing capabilities.
- Defense production upgrades: more than $275 million of the $1B total to upgrade sites producing defense engines and components, including:
  - Lynn, Massachusetts: $40+ million to refresh machinery, expand test cell capacity, and upgrade facilities.
  - Madisonville, Kentucky: $10 million for new machines, increased part production, inspection equipment, tooling, and upgrades.
- Commercial engine expansion (notably the CFM LEAP engines for Boeing 737 MAX and Airbus A320 families): $200 million to expand LEAP high-pressure turbine durability kit production and to support the reverse bleed system; $20 million in Durham, North Carolina for specialized tooling and engine line assembly systems; $7 million in Lafayette, Indiana for tools and facility upgrades to meet 2026 narrowbody deliveries.
- Supply chain strengthening: more than $100 million of the $1B to external suppliers for tooling and equipment to stabilize production and meet delivery commitments.

Operational metrics and context:
- FLIGHT DECK lean model contributed to >40% improvement in material input from priority suppliers year-over-year, driving 2025 engine deliveries up 25% (commercial) and 30% (defense) vs 2024.
- GE Aerospace Foundation program: $30 million to train 10,000 workers by 2030.
- Since 2024, GE Aerospace has announced >$2.5B in U.S. manufacturing investments, including about $600M in defense-engine sites over three years; annual R&D investment runs near $3B.
- CFM LEAP engines are produced by CFM International (GE Aerospace and Safran Aircraft Engines, 50-50 joint venture). LEAP powers Boeing 737 MAX and Airbus A320 family aircraft.
- Quote: H. Lawrence Culp, Jr., GE Aerospace Chairman and CEO, emphasizes continued U.S. leadership through investment.

Civil.title: Airbus opens 5,000-seater tech centre in Bengaluru
Civil.content:
Airbus opened a 5,000-seater technology centre on the outskirts of Bengaluru on March 6, 2026, as part of expanding its India footprint. The 880,000-square-foot Airbus India Technology Centre will function as a hub for engineering, digital transformation, customer services and procurement, reinforcing Airbus’s Make in India push. India now employs more than 30,000 Airbus personnel. Jürgen Westermeier, president and MD for India and South Asia, described it as a strategic acceleration—providing scale and headroom to grow and ensuring Indian expertise is woven into Airbus’ global value chains.

The Bengaluru centre is Airbus’s largest engineering and digital hub outside Europe and will cover the full aircraft lifecycle, including maintenance and optimisation of Airbus commercial aircraft and helicopter programmes. Indian engineers and digital specialists will work on critical technologies in cybersecurity, robotics and AI.

Civil Aviation Minister Rammohan Naidu Kinjarapu reaffirmed Bengaluru’s status as a global aviation hub and cited domestic and international confidence in India’s tech capabilities. Airbus has boosted annual sourcing from India from $500 million in 2019 to over $1.5 billion today, with projections to exceed $2 billion. The company works with more than 100 Indian suppliers supplying essential components for global aircraft programmes and supports final assembly lines for military transport aircraft and helicopters.

Deputy Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar stressed the potential of India’s young engineers and urged a stronger manufacturing presence beyond market activity, while Kinjarapu called for continued discussions on a second Bengaluru airport.

Civil.title: Embraer Proposes Indian Assembly Line for E175 Jets by 2028 Conditional on Securing at Least 200 Orders
Civil.content:
Embraer is proposing a final assembly line in India to produce E175-E1 regional jets, potentially starting as early as 2028, but only if it secures at least 200 aircraft offtake. CEO Francisco Gomes Neto told Reuters that orders must be in place before a meaningful investment is undertaken, with a target deadline of securing those 200 aircraft by the end of 2026 to enable deliveries in 2028—about a 24-month window to begin production.

The plan follows an MoU with India’s Adani Group announced earlier this year to establish a final assembly line for Embraer’s first-generation jetliners in India. Embraer has identified at least 1,800 Indian routes that could be operated by E1s, which seat up to 88 passengers and are central to U.S. regional aviation proliferation, though demand has varied elsewhere in recent years.

A India-based plant would help expand production while allowing Embraer’s Brazil-based hybrid production line to be filled with orders for the newer E2 family, which is enjoying strong global demand. The company had targeted 100 commercial aircraft deliveries in 2028 but now sees potential to reach that milestone in 2027.

On defense, Embraer also notes India as a strategic market via its Mahindra partnership on the C-390 military cargo jet. Saudi Arabia’s C-390 prospects have cooled; Gomes Neto said Saudi, the EU, and the US were previously “hotspots,” but the focus is shifting to India and the United States, with the Saudi deal for a C-390 assembly line via SAMI and PIF no longer central.

Civil.title: West Asia conflict disrupts aviation: Over 5,500 flights cancelled, says minister
Civil.content:
The Israel–US–Iran conflict has triggered airspace closures across West Asia, disrupting global aviation and forcing Indian and foreign carriers to suspend thousands of flights. As of March 16, 2026, Indian airlines have canceled 4,335 flights, while foreign carriers have canceled 1,187 flights, totaling 5,522 flight cancellations. The cancellations stem primarily from airspace shutoffs in parts of West Asia, which have compelled airlines to suspend or reroute services. Despite the disruptions, operations have continued where temporary slots or safe routes were available, with nearly 219,780 passengers still able to travel during the period.

Safety remains the government’s top priority; airlines cannot operate where airspace has been officially closed due to security risks. The Ministry of Civil Aviation and the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) are maintaining constant coordination with aviation regulators in affected countries. This coordination is aimed at ensuring that flights can resume quickly once airspace becomes available and safe for operations. Normal flight operations will only resume when the airspace is fully reopened and security conditions improve. The ongoing communications and regulatory alignment highlight how geopolitical disruptions directly impact route planning, airline capacity, and recovery timelines for both Indian and international carriers, with implications for capacity allocation, fleet utilization, and contingency routing in the region.

Defence.title: India pitches to join Future Combat Air System with France
Defence.content:
At the 6th India-France Annual Defence Dialogue in Bengaluru (February), India signaled its interest in joining France’s Future Combat Air System (FCAS) sixth-generation fighter programme, seeking co-development and co-manufacture of the FCAS fighter. The meeting was led by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and France’s Minister of the Armed Forces and Veterans Affairs, Catherine Vautrin. FCAS, launched by France and Germany in 2017 with Spain joining in 2019, aims to field a next-generation air combat system centered on a sixth-generation fighter, supplemented by unmanned systems and advanced network-centric warfare capabilities.

In parallel, India pitched for the export of its indigenous Pinaka Multi-Barrel Rocket Launcher (MBRL) to France; discussions reportedly progressed positively. India’s broader defence push continues alongside its own fifth-generation stealth aircraft programme, the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA). The government approved AMCA development in May 2025, with first flight expected around 2028–29 and induction planned by 2035; notably, the AMCA bid has been opened to private companies for the first time.

India’s previous fifth-generation effort, the FGFA with Russia, was discontinued in 2018. Separately, India’s defence exports reached a record ₹23,620 crore, with sales to over 100 nations, including the United States, France and Armenia. The government aims to achieve ₹3 lakh crore in defence manufacturing and ₹50,000 crore in defence exports by 2029. The FCAS talks mark a significant expansion of India–France defence-industrial collaboration and broader regional and global implications for advanced combat-air systems.

Defence.title: ADA Validates Advanced Intake Aerodynamics for AMCA, Research Achieves 98% Pressure Recovery for Stealth Aircraft
Defence.content:
ADA (Aeronautical Development Agency) has validated a new S-duct intake geometry for stealth propulsion, a key enabler for India’s Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) program. The results, published in the February 2026 edition of the Journal of Aerospace Sciences and Technologies, combine wind-tunnel testing and CFD to address the S-duct challenge of concealing compressor blades while maintaining engine performance. The study, authored by researchers including R. Abilashini and Valliammai Somasundaram, demonstrates two major milestones: 98% pressure recovery at transonic speeds (near Mach 1), meaning the engine receives dense, stable air for maximum combat power; and extreme maneuverability with stability at a 60-degree angle of attack, due to a lip-generated controlled vortex that guides flow smoothly into the duct during tight turns.

Innovation in testing is notable: truncated (scaled) models can yield 100% accurate intake behavior data if mass-flow instrumentation is correctly calibrated. The researchers also developed correction factors to eliminate Sting Interference, enhancing real-world data accuracy in wind-tunnel tests.

Strategically, the work supports AMCA and provides foundational data for future sixth-generation tailless or blended wing-body aircraft, where lack of vertical stabilizers raises flight-control challenges. The article highlights broader defense implications: the MoD invites domestic bids to integrate next-gen missiles and helmet-mounted displays into the IAF’s 74 Jaguar fleet; HAL is seeking a 95–100 kN engine for the HLFT-42 trainer to align with Tejas Mk2, sidelining the Kaveri for primary propulsion.

Key program terms: AMCA, S-duct, Tailless/ blended wing-body concepts.

Defence.title: India investing in next-gen tech, transforming how defence solutions are conceived: Rajnath Singh
Defence.content:
Union Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said India is rapidly turning into a hub of defence innovation and is investing in next-generation technologies to transform how solutions are conceived and developed. Speaking virtually to a two-day roundtable for defence attaches at Rashtriya Raksha University (RRU) in Gandhinagar, he highlighted the theme “Aatmanirbhar Bharat in the Global Defence Tech Landscape: Accelerating Innovation, Exports, and Joint Technology Partnerships.” The event gathered defence diplomats and representatives from 24 nations across Africa, Asia, the Pacific, and the Caribbean.

Singh stressed that India’s long-term trajectory under Atmanirbhar Bharat aims for self-reliance while remaining globally connected. India is investing in AI, unmanned systems, space, and advanced digital capabilities, underscoring that technological progress cannot flourish in isolation. He warned that warfare is evolving into cyber and hybrid domains, necessitating deeper international cooperation. Sustainable security, he said, is built through partnership, co-development, knowledge sharing, training, and collaborative capability building. India’s expanding network of defence engagements across regions reflects this approach, leveraging dialogue, joint exercises, and industrial cooperation to promote a secure, open, and inclusive international order.

The defence-attache community was described as a vital bridge between military, government, and industry. Singh reiterated Modi’s vision of India as a ‘vishwa mitra’—a trusted friend and partner to the world—guided by dialogue, innovation, and partnership in defence and security.

Defence.title: India 2nd largest importer of arms in 2021–25, accounted for 8.2% of global arms receipts, think tank says
Defence.content:
SIPRI’s 2021–25 arms transfer study shows India as the world’s second-largest arms importer, accounting for 8.2% of global arms imports. Although India is shifting its arms relations away from Russia toward Western suppliers (France, Israel, USA), Moscow remained the largest supplier, though Russia’s share of India’s imports fell to 40% in 2021–25 from 70% in 2011–15. Overall, India’s defence imports declined 4% between 2016–20 and 2021–25, reflecting growing domestic design/production capability but continued reliance on foreign sources for offsets and capability gaps.

Global context: Ukraine, India, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Pakistan were the top five defence importers, collectively receiving 35% of global arms imports in 2021–25; the five largest global suppliers (USA, France, Russia, Germany, China) supplied 70% of exports, with USA exports rising 27% and its share from 36% to 42% of global arms exports. Russia’s share dropped to 6.8% in 2021–25 from 21% in 2016–20.

Key India defense initiatives and partnerships:
- April 2025: Inter-Governmental Agreement with France for 26 Rafale aircraft for the Indian Navy (22 Single-Seaters, 4 Twin-Seaters) including training, simulators, associated equipment, weapons, and performance-based logistics; delivery by 2030; crew training in France and India.
- Prior/ongoing: 26 Rafale-Marine aircraft contract with France; Scorpène (P75 Kalvari) program, 6th submarine delivered Jan 15, 2025; continued submarine cooperation.
- US: 10-year framework for US–India major defence partnership; defence secretary Pete Hegseth called India a strategic priority.
- Wet-lease agreement with Metrea Management for one KC-135 air-to-air refuelling aircraft; delivery to FRA within six months for IAF/Navy training.
- Indigenous & industrial: Safran–HAL IMRH development; MRO for M-88 engines; Safran–BEL HAMMER missiles in India; Airbus H125 final assembly line with ATA Advanced Systems.
- 2,182 crore contract with Rosoboronexport for Surface-to-Air Vertical Launch Shtil missiles and frames.
- Domestic manufacturing: Rs 7.85 lakh crore defence allocation for FY27 (up 15.19% vs BE FY2025–26), 14.67% of Union Budget; Rs 1.39 lakh crore for domestic procurement; 75% of capital acquisitions reserved for domestic suppliers; overall defence budget rose from Rs 2.53 lakh crore (2013–14) to Rs 7.85 lakh crore (2026–27).

Defence.title: Gujarat to form SPV for defence testing, industry linkages | Ahmedabad News - The Times of India
Defence.content:
Gujarat is moving to form a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) to establish a defence testing laboratory and related facilities, creating a permanent link between local industry and India’s defence forces. The SPV, to be overseen by the state’s Industry & Mines department, will boost defence supply production in Gujarat and serve as a full-time bridge between local MSMEs and the Army, Navy, and Air Force. A dedicated budget has been allocated for the SPV, though the article does not specify the amount.

Mamta Verma, additional chief secretary for Industry & Mines, noted that Gujarat’s MSMEs and other industries already supply equipment to the armed forces, but the state’s potential remains largely untapped across all services. A detailed study found that despite adequate capacity, local industries miss opportunities due to limited access to defence establishments and gaps in technical knowledge. The proposed testing laboratory will test and certify products developed by local units and provide training on defence procurement requirements.

The government plans to introduce special incentives for MSMEs under upcoming industrial and defence & aerospace policies. It will also launch industry-defence connect initiatives to help the defence forces articulate their needs, enabling local manufacturers to develop and supply suitable products. The move, reported by Kapil Dave of The Times of India on March 17, 2026, signals Gujarat’s intent to strengthen domestic defence sourcing and accelerate local capabilities.

Defence.title: 13-Ton Ghatak UCAV Receives Critical Development Clearance, Poised to Become IAF's Primary Stealth Strike Platform
Defence.content:
India’s Defence Procurement Board cleared the design and development of the 13-ton Ghatak Unmanned Combat Aerial Vehicle (UCAV), spearheaded by DRDO, signaling a strategic leap for the IAF’s deep-strike and electronic-warfare capabilities. Marketed as a “first wave” stealth asset, Ghatak is intended to penetrate contested airspace before manned fighters to execute Suppression and Destruction of Enemy Air Defences (SEAD/DEAD). Its tailless flying-wing configuration, serpentine air intakes, and an internal weapons bay are designed to minimize radar signature and carry precision-guided munitions without external pylons. The program envisions a networked sensor-strike node with an AESA radar and advanced EO/IR sensors to autonomously detect, track, and strike targets deep inside adversary territory.

Technical and propulsion specifics:
- Class: 13-ton UCAV (heavyweight)
- Propulsion: Indigenous Kaveri engine (dry, non-afterburning) delivering ~49 kN thrust
- Endurance: Combat radius >1,000 km; loiter time 5–8 hours
- Payload: Internal payload ~1.5 tons
- Primary role: Stealth strike/SEAD
- Platform evolution: From SWIFT (Stealth Wing Flying Testbed) to a 13-ton demonstrator; demonstrates confidence in tailless flight control laws

Strategic implications:
- Addresses an imminent capability gap as IAF retires SEPECAT Jaguar deep-penetration strikes over the next decade.
- By removing a pilot in initial conflict hours, enhances risk-free deep-strike operations against modern IADS.
- If successful, positions India among the U.S., Russia, and China in indigenous stealth UCAV capability, boosting domestic defence manufacturing.

Contextual comparison: Ghatak’s projected metrics (radius >1,000 km, loiter 5–8 hours, internal ~1.5 t) contrast with HAL Tejas Mk1A (radius 300–500 km; external payload 3.5–5 t).

Defence.title: Union Minister Piyush Goyal highlights the rapid rise of India’s startup ecosystem in defence, space sectors
Defence.content: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal told the 66th cohort of the National Defence College in New Delhi on March 7, 2026, that India’s startup ecosystem in defence and space is rising rapidly, powered by MSMEs that are integrating Indian innovation into global supply chains. He framed this under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s speed, skill, and scale mantra, calling it a cornerstone of India’s self-reliance in defence. In remarks tied to the policy theme “Boosting India’s Manufacturing Sector: Role of Government and Policy,” Goyal highlighted the ongoing role of government and policy in accelerating manufacturing and noted the strategic importance of semiconductors and clean energy to advance self-reliance. The message underscores a shift toward indigenous capability and global integration through MSMEs, with the rapid ascent of defence and space startups positioned to strengthen domestic supply chains and broaden India’s manufacturing footprint. These developments align with broader government priorities to enhance manufacturing competitiveness and integrate Indian innovation into global defense supply networks. The focus on semiconductors and clean energy signals strategic thrusts for long-term self-reliance in critical technologies.

Defence.title: Amid conflicts, countries will have to build their industrial complex, upgrade tech: Navy chief
Defence.content:
At Raisina Dialogue 2026 in New Delhi, Navy Chief Admiral Dinesh K. Tripathi warned that in today’s conflicts nations must build their own industrial complexes, upgrade technology while production continues, and be prepared for rapid adaptation and surge capability. Speaking on the panel “Forgers of Peace: Ordnance Factories for the Liberal Order,” he said the idea of short, decisive wars is being questioned and the post-Cold War peace dividend has ended, making national security self-reliance a priority. Countries are developing domestic industrial bases, often in partnership with others, to meet evolving threats.

For India, Tripathi emphasized self-reliance alongside co-development and co-production with partner nations, rather than relying solely on external sources. He noted Russia is one partner among others, but India is pursuing indigenous solutions, with a focus on niche technologies through structured collaborations. He stated the Navy is backing Make in India and expects to become self-reliant in coming years, combining indigenous production and development with targeted international cooperation.

The dialogue—India’s premier geopolitics and geo-economics conference—was organized by the Observer Research Foundation with the Ministry of External Affairs and marked by the 11th edition, inaugurated in the presence of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Other panelists included Lt Gen Susan Coyle (Australia) on deterrence by denial and Benedikta Von Seherr-Thoss (EEAS) on forging international partnerships, underscoring global capacity constraints and the need for partnerships in defense capacity building. Implications for aviation/defense firms include expanding domestic production, accelerating tech refresh, and pursuing diversified co-development and Make in India strategies to sustain competitive advantage.

Defence.title: West Asia conflict: US President Donald Trump asks defence contractors to quadruple production
Defence.content:
US President Donald Trump has asked defence contractors to quadruple production in response to the West Asia conflict, according to a DH Web Desk report. The article notes that a meeting on the matter included major defence primes: Lockheed Martin, Raytheon Technologies (RTX), BAE Systems, Boeing, Honeywell Aerospace, L3Harris Technologies, and Northrop Grumman. The piece was published and last updated on 07 March 2026 at 03:19 IST.

Key facts preserved in the report include:
- The core directive: quadrupling production to address the West Asia security situation.
- Attendees: Lockheed Martin; RTX (Raytheon Technologies); BAE Systems; Boeing; Honeywell Aerospace; L3Harris Technologies; Northrop Grumman.
- Dates/timestamps: published and last updated 07 March 2026, 03:19 IST.
- Source category: Defence; mentions Iran in metadata/keywords.

What is not disclosed in the excerpt:
- No dollar figures, percentages, or specific production targets.
- No timelines, contract details, or material/product names beyond the company roster.
- No breakdown of sectors (air, land, naval) or which programs would be affected.

Strategic takeaway for aviation/defence intelligence:
- The administration’s push to significantly scale up output involves the largest U.S. defense primes, signaling a broad ramp-up across major platforms and systems. The absence of price or program specifics in the excerpt suggests the article is reporting the directive and participant list rather than detailing contracts or line-item requirements.

SMR/ Nuclear.title: Expert Explains | How thorium can power India’s 100 GWe by 2047 mission
SMR/ Nuclear.content:
India’s thorium advantage is framed as central to achieving a 100 GWe nuclear mission by 2047, with the SHANTI Act 2025 viewed as a pivotal enabler. India holds the world’s largest thorium reserves, and thorium use offers energy independence and virtually eliminates proliferation risk. The SHANTI Act opens nuclear energy to public/private sectors, academia and industry, but a conducive regulatory framework is also essential to realize it.

The 100 GWe by 2047 mission would be powered largely by thermal reactors and would require about 18,000–20,000 tonnes of mined uranium annually—roughly one-third of current global production. With global capacity rising from about 380 GWe today to around 1,400 GWe, known uranium resources (~8 million tonnes) could sustain once-through use for only about three decades, underscoring uranium-supply fragility.

Two conclusions follow: uranium in once-through mode is unsustainable, and securing a share of global uranium supply will become harder. The solution is nuclear recycling; thorium recycling increases fuel energy potential by 50–100x. India, with the world’s largest thorium reserves, could gain energy independence and reduce proliferation risk through thorium cycles, but challenges remain and require a large, innovative effort.

India’s three-stage plan aims to use fast breeders (FBRs) after thermal reactors. The first 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor is almost ready. Beyond that, metal-fuelled FBRs with fuel recycling must be developed, but rapid capacity growth is realistically still about three decades away. In the interim, the 100 GWe goal—largely uranium-driven—drives PHWR expansion beyond 10 GWe. A key opportunity is irradiating thorium in PHWRs using HALEU (high-assay low-enriched uranium) to produce U-233 for third-stage Thorium Molten Salt Reactor (TMSR)–based SMRs. This could be done with minimal PHWR design changes and would improve economics, safety and back-end costs.

Qualifying HALEU–thorium fuel requires accelerated irradiation testing in PHWRs; India lacks such facilities but can leverage international cooperation agreements. HALEU supply chains are evolving worldwide, with China taking the lead. The 2025–26 budget regards SMR development as a priority, alongside TMSR; SMRs could also produce low-cost green hydrogen via direct thermochemical routes, and share a back-end pyrochemical recycling process with irradiated HALEU–thorium fuel.

Overall, the SHANTI ecosystem is viewed as essential to mobilize thorium-based pathways, accelerate U-233 production, and advance SMR and TMSR development toward India’s energy-security and defense-industrial objectives.

SMR/ Nuclear.title: How thorium can power India’s 100 GWe by 2047 mission | Current Affairs | Vision IAS
SMR/ Nuclear.content:
India’s SHANTI Act 2025 is poised to transform its atomic energy landscape by opening the sector to public/private, academia and industry, while signaling that a supportive regulatory framework free from monopolies is essential for development. The piece highlights uranium-supply constraints: to reach 100 GWe of nuclear capacity by 2047, India would need about 18,000–20,000 tonnes of uranium annually, roughly one-third of today’s global production, with global reactor capacity projected to 1,400 GWe by 2047. Existing uranium resources could sustain growth for only about three decades under a once-through cycle, underscoring the unsustainability of uranium-only expansion.

Thorium recycling is presented as a strategic alternative. India houses the world’s largest thorium reserves, offering energy independence and reduced proliferation risk. A multidisciplinary effort is required to overcome technical hurdles, with India’s three-stage programme hinging on Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs); the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor is nearing completion, and metal-fuelled FBRs with recycling must be developed to support rapid growth. While the current focus is on the 100 GWe mission using imported uranium, Pressurized Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) can be leveraged to produce uranium-233 for third-stage thorium reactors. The combination of thorium with High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) in PHWRs is cited for improved fuel economics, safety, and proliferation resistance.

International cooperation is needed to advance HALEU-thorium fuel development, as India lacks accelerated irradiation testing facilities. The strategy also calls for development of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) and low-cost green hydrogen systems, potentially sharing back-end technologies such as pyrochemical recycling. The piece warns that China’s SMR progress pressures India to prioritize this area, as noted in the 2025–26 budget. In sum, SHANTI Act 2025 aims to catalyze energy independence, per a former Atomic Energy Commission chairman.
